text: Grace Medes (November 9, 1886 – December 31, 1967) was an American biochemist who discovered tyrosinosis, a metabolic disorder now known as tyrosinemia, and studied fatty acid metabolism. She was awarded the Garvan-Olin Medal in 1955 for her contributions to chemistry. Grace May Medes was born in Keokuk, Iowa, as the daughter of William Johnson Medes and Kate Francisco Hagny Medes. She earned her bachelor's and master's degrees in zoology from the University of Kansas and a PhD in 1916 from Bryn Mawr College. After completing her PhD, she taught at Vassar College starting in 1916 as an instructor in zoology until 1919, then as an assistant professor of physiology until 1922, becoming the first female faculty member with a PhD in the physiology department there. She moved to Wellesley College in 1922, serving as associate professor of physiology until 1924, and then joined the University of Minnesota Medical School in 1924 as a fellow for her first year and later as an assistant professor until 1932. During her time at Minnesota, she discovered the human metabolic disorder she named "tyrosinosis" in 1932; although her patient was atypical and the mechanism she identified has since been questioned, her testing methods remain a useful model for current research on tyrosinemia. In 1932, she became head of the department of metabolic chemistry at the Lankenau Institute for Medical Research in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where she specialized in sulfur and fatty acid metabolism, establishing foundational work that contributed to the later discovery of Coenzyme A. She remained a research faculty member at the institute, later merged with the Institute for Cancer Research, until 1952, serving as a senior member from 1954 to 1960. In 1955, she received the Garvan Medal (now the Garvan-Olin Medal) from the American Chemical Society as an outstanding woman in chemistry and was also named one of the year's five distinguished alumni by the University of Kansas. In retirement, she resumed her work on tyrosinosis at the Fels Research Institute at Temple University and co-authored the book Normal Growth and Cancer in 1963 with Stanley P. Reimann. A symposium on tyrosinosis was held in Oslo, Norway, in her honor in 1965. Medes died on December 31, 1967, at the age of 81.
